info.title: Quiver API

get.description: Returns all registered arrows. Use the WebSocket upgrade to stream real-time updates instead.
Returns detailed information for an arrow including current state, active run, and last return. Use the WebSocket upgrade to stream live updates.

post.description: Registers an arrow by its namespace. The manifest must already exist in the registry.

delete.description: Deregisters an arrow. The namespace must include a @ref (version) qualifier.

patch.description: Fetches the latest manifest for the arrow and updates its registration.

get.description: Returns the full manifest definition including targets, variables, and lifecycle steps.

post.description: Accepts a raw YAML manifest in the request body, stores it in the registry, and registers the arrow. Use this to publish a new arrow from a local manifest file.
Parses and validates a raw YAML manifest. Returns validation errors and platform compatibility without writing anything to the registry.

get.description: Returns quiver collections. Use ?followed=true for followed only, ?followed=false for unfollowed cached, or omit for all.
Returns detailed information for a quiver including its arrows and follow status.

post.description: Follows a quiver collection and caches its arrows locally.

get.description: Returns the raw cached manifest for a quiver.

post.description: Stores a raw quiver manifest (YAML or QUIVER.md) for the given namespace.
Validates a raw quiver manifest without storing it.

get.description: Returns {"status":"ok"} when the daemon is running.

post.description: Triggers a lifecycle method on an arrow (install, uninstall, execute, stop, update, or any custom method defined in the manifest). Returns 202 Accepted immediately; progress is streamed via WebSocket.

parameters.description: Method name (install | uninstall | execute | stop | update | <custom>)
parameters.name: method

get.description:
Searches everything this machine already knows about: arrows installed, arrows pulled in as dependencies, arrows from followed collections, and every arrow Quiver has resolved recently. The search is offline and always answers — it never reaches the network.

Results are ranked by textual relevance, then boosted for an exact name match, membership of a followed collection, and stars. Installed state, provenance and known versions are reported, never scored.

The os filter is advisory: the compatible-OS list is a denormalised projection of the last compile, and install-time re-resolution is authoritative. Treat it as a hint, not a gate.

parameters.description: Search text. Empty or whitespace-only is rejected.
parameters.name: q

parameters.description: Maximum results to return. Defaults to 25, capped at 100.
parameters.name: limit

400.description: Missing q, or an unknown os value

post.description:
Searches the configured git hosts for arrows nobody on this machine has seen yet, and returns immediately with a job id. It does not wait for providers.

Every candidate is proven before it is reported: its manifest is fetched, parsed and compiled, then written to the vault. That is what makes the results renderable without a second round trip, and what makes a later POST /v0/arrow/{ns} on a discovered namespace serve from cache.

Verified results stream from GET /v0/search/discover/{job} with an Upgrade header. Counts and per-provider failures never appear on that stream; read them once from the same path without the header, after the socket closes.

parameters.description: Query. Blank or whitespace-only is rejected.
parameters.name: body

400.description: Missing or blank q, or a body that is not JSON

503.description: Discovery is not configured on this daemon

get.description:
Returns the status of a discovery pass and, once it has finished, how many candidates were found, verified and skipped, plus what every host contributed.

A host that refused is reported with the reason and, for a rate limit, how many seconds to wait. That is the only place a client can tell "GitHub rate-limited you" apart from "nothing matched", because the result stream carries results and nothing else.

Read this once, when the socket closes. Do not poll it. A finished job stays readable for a short grace period and is then evicted, after which this returns 404 and the search should simply be run again — the verified manifests are already in the vault.

Sending an Upgrade: websocket header to this same path opens the result stream instead.

503.description: Discovery is not configured on this daemon

expires_at.description:
ExpiresAt is when the job stops being readable. While the pass is still
running it is a floor, not a promise: the grace is measured from the
moment the pass finishes.

retry_after.description:
RetryAfter is in seconds and is set only when the host said how long to
wait.

compatible_os.description:
CompatibleOS is a denormalised projection of the last compile and is
advisory: install-time re-resolution is authoritative.

known.description:
Known says the arrow is already on this machine. Every GET /v0/search
result is known by construction; a streamed result is known when the
catalog already held it. A client merging streamed results over an
already-rendered list must keep its own row when this is true, or it
will overwrite a correct provenance with a less specific one.

media.description: Media is the icon/banner pair declared by the manifest.

provenance.description:
Provenance is empty when the server cannot say: a streamed result the
catalog already holds is known to be yours, but discovery does not know
which provenance your catalog recorded for it.

versions.description: Versions are the refs known locally, not every ref that exists upstream.

resolved_branch.description:
ResolvedBranch is where the manifest physically came from, which differs
from InstalledRef whenever the namespace carried no ref: the ref is what
was asked for, the branch is what the default-branch list settled on.
Empty means unknown, which resolves through the list as before.

upgraded_from_ns.description:
UpgradedFromNs is set only on the arrow.upgraded.* event; it names the
old namespace that was replaced so the runtime reaction can clean up.
